'''Colin Llewellyn Raston''' {{post-nominals|country=AUS|AO|FAA}} (born 1950) is a Professor of Chemistry of [[Flinders University]] in Adelaide, South Australia and the [[Premier of South Australia|Premier's]] Professorial Fellow in Clean Technology.<ref name = FlindersBio />  In 2015, he was awarded an [[Ig Nobel Prize]] in "for inventing a chemical recipe to partially un-boil an egg".<ref name = IgNobel>{{cite web|title = Improbable Research – The 2015 Ig Nobel Prize Winners|date = 17 September 2015|url = http://www.improbable.com/ig/winners/#ig2015|website = www.improbable.com|accessdate = 15 June 2016}}</ref>  In 2016, Raston was made an Officer of the Order of Australia for his services to science.<ref name = AO />

== Research work ==
=== Early career ===
[[File:ArsenobetainePIC.svg|thumb|left|200px|Chemical structure of [[arsenobetaine]] ]]
Raston undertook his early tertiary studies at [[the University of Western Australia]], taking a [[bachelor degree]] in science with honours and a [[doctor of philosophy]] under Professor Allan White.<ref name = FlindersBio />
Raston's work included looking at marine [[organoarsenic compound]]s, isolating [[arsenobetaine]] from the [[Western Rock Lobster]] and determining its structure and synthesis.<ref>{{cite journal|last1 = Edmonds|first1 = J. S.|last2 = Francesconi|first2 = K. A.|last3 = Cannon|first3 = J. R.|last4 = Raston|first4 = C. L.|last5 = Skelton|first5 = B. W.|last6 = White|first6 = A. H.|title = Isolation, crystal structure and Synthesis of arsenobetaine, the arsenical constituent of the Western Rock Lobster ''Panulirus longipes cygnus'' George|journal = [[Tetrahedron Letters]]|year = 1977|volume = 18|issue = 18|pages = 1543–1546|doi = 10.1016/S0040-4039(01)93098-9}}</ref>  This [[zwitterion]]ic substance turns out to be the main source of [[arsenic]] in [[fish]]<ref>{{cite journal|first = K. A.|last = Francesconi|title = Current perspectives in arsenic environmental and biological research|journal = [[Environmental Chemistry (journal)|Environmental Chemistry]]|year = 2005|volume = 2|issue = 3|pages = 141–145|doi = 10.1071/EN05042}}</ref> and unlike other arsenic compounds (like [[dimethylarsine]] and [[trimethylarsine]]) it has comparatively low toxicity.<ref>{{cite journal|last1 = Bhattacharya|first1 = P.|last2 = Welch|first2 = A. H.|last3 = Stollenwerk|first3 = K. G.|last4 = McLaughlin|first4 = M. J.|last5 = Bundschuh|first5 = J.|last6 = Panaullah|first6 = G.|title = Arsenic in the environment: Biology and chemistry|journal = [[Science of the Total Environment]]|year = 2007|volume = 379|issue = 2–3|pages = 109–120|doi = 10.1016/j.scitotenv.2007.02.037|pmid=17434206|bibcode = 2007ScTEn.379..109B}}</ref>  Arsenobetaine is an [[analog (chemistry)|analog]] of betaine ([[trimethylglycine]]) and with similar [[biosynthesis]] to [[choline]] and [[betaine]]s.<ref>{{cite journal|first1 = B. M.|last1 = Adair|first2 = S. B.|last2 = Waters|first3 = V.|last3 = Devesa|first4 = Z.|last4 = Drobna|first5 = M.|last5 = Styblo|first6 = D. J.|last6 = Thomas|title = Commonalities in metabolism of arsenicals|journal = [[Environmental Chemistry (journal)|Environmental Chemistry]]|year = 2005|volume = 2|issue = 3|pages = 161–166|doi = 10.1071/EN05054|url = https://zenodo.org/record/1236044}}</ref>

He later received a [[higher doctorate]] ([[Doctor of Science]]) from Griffith University.<ref name = FlindersBio />

=== Calixarenes ===
[[File:Calixarene.png|250px|thumb|right|[[calixarene|Calix[4]arene]] with ''para''-''tert''-butyl substituents and a [[hydrophobic]] cavity formed by the phenyl groups. [[Hydrogen bonding]] between the [[hydroxyl]] groups stabilises the 'base' of the chalice.]]
[[Resorcinarene]] is a [[macrocycle]] typically prepared by the [[condensation reaction|condensation]] of [[resorcinol]] and [[formaldehyde]] in an acidic environment.  Multiple isomers are possible when any other [[aldehyde]] is used and different conditions, including [[Lewis acid]] [[catalysis]] have been employed to minimise [[by-products]].<ref>{{cite journal|last = Högberg|first = A. G. S.|title = Two stereoisomeric macrocyclic resorcinol-acetaldehyde condensation products|journal = [[Journal of Organic Chemistry]]|volume = 45|issue = 22|year = 1980|pages = 4498–4500|doi = 10.1021/jo01310a046}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last = Högberg|first = A. G. S.|title = Cyclooligomeric phenol-aldehyde condensation products. 2. Stereoselective synthesis and DNMR study of two 1,8,15,22-tetraphenyl[14]metacyclophan-3,5,10,12,17,19,24,26-octols|journal = [[Journal of the American Chemical Society]]|volume = 102|issue = 19|year = 1980|pages = 6046–6050|doi = 10.1021/ja00539a012| bibcode=1980JAChS.102.6046H }}</ref> Raston and co-workers have developed an alternative [[green chemistry]] solvent-free approach whereby resorcinol and the aldehyde are ground together with [[p-Toluenesulfonic acid|''p''-toluenesulfonic acid]] in a [[mortar and pestle]] and the product [[Recrystallization (chemistry)|recrystallised]] from the resulting paste.<ref name = GreenCalixarene>{{cite journal|last1 = Antesberger|first1 = J|last2 = Cave|first2 = G. W.|last3 = Ferrarelli|first3 = M. C.|last4 = Heaven|first4 = M. W.|last5 = Raston|first5 = C. L.|last6 = Atwood|first6 = J. L.|title = Solvent-free, direct synthesis of supramolecular nano-capsules|journal = [[Chemical Communications]]|volume = 2005|issue = 7|year = 2005|pages = 892–894|doi = 10.1039/b412251h|pmid=15700072}}</ref>
:[[File:Resorcinarene synth.svg]]

[[Calixarene]]s are the general category of macrocycle [[oligomer]]s formed by hydroxyalkylation of a [[phenol]] and an aldehyde;<ref>{{cite book|authorlink1=C. David Gutsche|last = Gutsche|first = C. D.|title = Calixarenes|location = Cambridge|publisher = [[Royal Society of Chemistry]]|year = 1989|isbn = 085186385X}}</ref> Resorcinarenes are one example.  Calixarenes resemble [[Chalice (cup)|chalice]]s (calix in [[Latin]]) with [[hydrophobic]] cavities that can hold smaller molecules or ions, an example of [[host–guest chemistry]].  Raston has demonstrated a green chemistry approach to pyrogallol[4]arene from [[isovaleraldehyde]] (3-methylbutanal) and [[pyrogallol]] (1,2,3-benzenetriol) with a catalytic amount of ''p''-toluenesulfonic acid.<ref name = GreenCalixarene />  He also produced a ball-and-socket [[supramolecular chemistry|supramolecular complex]] where calix[5]arene hosts the C<sub>70</sub> [[fullerene]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1 = Atwood|first1 = J. L.|last2 = Barbour|first2 = L. J.|last3 = Heaven|first3 = M. W.|last4 = Raston|first4 = C. L.|title = Association and orientation of C<sub>70</sub> on complexation with calix[5]arene|journal = [[Chemical Communications]]|year = 2003|volume = 2003|issue = 18|pages = 2270–2271|doi = 10.1039/B306411P|pmid=14518869}}</ref>  The five phenyl groups forming the walls of the cavity interact with the [[aromaticity|aromatic]] fullerene through [[pi stacking|π stacking]].

=== Unboiling an egg ===
Ovalbumin is the protein which makes up around two-thirds of the white of an egg.<ref>{{cite journal|last1 = Huntington|first1 = J. A.|last2 = Stein|first2 = P. E.|year = 2001|title = Structure and properties of ovalbumin|journal = [[Journal of Chromatography B]]|volume = 756|issue = 1–2|pages = 189–198|doi = 10.1016/S0378-4347(01)00108-6|pmid=11419711}}</ref>  When an egg is cooked, the ovalbumin [[conformational change|changes conformation]] from its [[protein folding|folded]] and soluble form to an insoluble all-[[β-sheet]] structure with exposed [[hydrophobic]] regions, leading to [[protein aggregation|aggregation]].<ref>{{Cite journal|first1 = H. Y.|last1 = Hu|first2 = H. N.|last2 = Du|title = α-to-β Structural transformation of ovalbumin: Heat and pH effects|journal = [[Journal of Protein Chemistry]]|year = 2000|pages = 177–183|volume = 19|issue = 3|doi = 10.1023/A:1007099502179|pmid=10981809| s2cid=82745511 }}</ref> This is a classic example of [[denaturation (biochemistry)|protein denaturation]], defined as the loss of the [[quaternary structure|quaternary]], [[tertiary structure|tertiary]] and [[secondary structure|secondary]] structures that are present in the protein's [[native state]], by application of some external chemical or radiative stress (including [[heat]]).<ref>{{cite book|title = Mosby's Medical Dictionary|url = http://medical-dictionary.thefreedictionary.com/Denaturation+%28biochemistry%29|accessdate = 14 June 2016|edition = 9th|year = 2009|publisher = [[Elsevier]]}}</ref> In order to "unboil" the egg, the individual protein strands must be separated from the aggregate and then re-folded back to their native form.<ref>{{cite journal|title = Shear-stress-mediated refolding of proteins from aggregates and inclusion Bodies|first1 = T. Z.|last1 = Yuan|first2 = C. F. G.|last2 = Ormonde|first3 = S. T.|last3 = Kudlacek|first4 = S.|last4 = Kunche|first5 = J. N.|last5 = Smith|first6 = W. A.|last6 = Brown|first7 = K. M.|last7 = Pugliese|first8 = T. J.|last8 = Olsen|first9 = M.|last9 = Iftikhar|first10 = C. L.|last10 = Raston|first11 = G. A.|last11 = Weiss|journal = [[ChemBioChem]]|volume = 16|issue = 3|pages = 393–396|year =  2015|doi = 10.1002/cbic.201402427|pmid=25620679|pmc=4388321}}</ref> Raston had the idea of using mechanical energy from spinning the aggregate to achieve this and developed [[vortex fluidic technology]] to implement his idea.<ref name = NewsCorp>{{cite news|url = https://www.news.com.au/technology/science/flinders-university-chemistry-professor-colin-raston-awarded-ig-nobel-prize-for-research-that-showed-how-to-unboil-an-egg/news-story/c9e5c495306592d1c7397b7a4c455b84|title = Over-cooked? Flinders University professor Colin Raston gets Ig Nobel Prize for 'unboiling an egg'|date = 23 September 2015|access-date = 14 June 2016|last = Seidel|first = J.|website = news.com.au|publisher = [[News Corporation (1980–2013)|News Corporation]]}}</ref> Using it to unboil an egg (at least in part) was meant as a demonstration of the technology and won Raston and colleagues the 2015 [[Ig Nobel Prize]] in chemistry.<ref name = IgNobel /> Applications of the technology include boosting the potency of anti-cancer drugs like [[carboplatin]]<ref>{{cite news|title = Machine that 'uncooks eggs' used to improve cancer treatment|last = Strom|first = M.|date = 22 May 2015|accessdate = 14 June 2016|url = http://www.smh.com.au/technology/sci-tech/machine-that-uncooks-eggs-used-to-improve-cancer-treatment-20150521-gh6gj4.html|newspaper = [[Sydney Morning Herald]]}}</ref> and improving the production of [[biodiesel]].<ref>{{cite news|url = http://www.abc.net.au/news/2015-05-22/unboil-egg-vortex-fluidic-cancer-drug-efficacy/6491078|publisher = [[Australian Broadcasting Corporation|ABC (Australia)]]|title = Cancer drug more effective after use of vortex fluidic device invented by Australian researcher|last = Eacott|first = A.|date = 22 May 2015|accessdate = 14 June 2016|website = abc.net.au}}</ref>

== Honours and awards ==
Raston was recognised for his professional achievements with Fellowships in the [[Royal Australian Chemical Institute]] (RACI) and the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]].<ref name = FlindersBio />  On 13 June 2016, [[Governor-General of Australia|Governor-General]], [[Peter Cosgrove|Sir Peter Cosgrove]] announced that Raston had been made an Officer of the Order of Australia in the [[2016 Queen's Birthday Honours (Australia)|Queen's Birthday Honours List]], for "distinguished service to science through seminal contributions to the field of chemistry as a researcher and academic, and to professional associations".<ref name = AO>{{cite web|title = The Queen's Birthday 2016 Honours List: Officer (AO) in the General Division of the Order of Australia|url = http://www.gg.gov.au/sites/default/files/files/honours/qb/qb2016/nS_29ods1A/Media%20Notes%20-%20AO.pdf|publisher = [[Governor-General of the Commonwealth of Australia]]|accessdate = 14 June 2016|page = 41|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160615121237/http://www.gg.gov.au/sites/default/files/files/honours/qb/qb2016/nS_29ods1A/Media%20Notes%20-%20AO.pdf|archive-date = 15 June 2016|url-status = dead}}</ref>

Raston served as the Vice President of the RACI in 1995–96, winning the H. G. Smith Memorial Medal that year,<ref name = FlindersBio>{{cite web|title = Professor Colin Raston|url = http://www.flinders.edu.au/people/colin.raston|publisher = [[Flinders University]]|accessdate = 16 June 2016}}</ref> and went on to serve as President the following year.<ref name = RACI>{{cite web|url = https://www.raci.org.au/document/item/1381|title = Royal Australian Chemical Institute Awards and Office Bearers|publisher = [[Royal Australian Chemical Institute]]|accessdate = 15 June 2016|archive-date = 7 March 2016|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160307083459/https://www.raci.org.au/document/item/1381|url-status = dead}}</ref>  He has received several RACI awards, including the Burrows Award in 1994, which is the premier award of the Inorganic Chemistry Division of the RACI. In 2002, he was recognised with the Green Chemistry Challenge Award and went on to take the Leighton Memorial Medal,<ref name = RACI /> the institute's most prestigious medal given in recognition of eminent services to chemistry in Australia, in 2006.  He was named an RACI Living Luminary and in 2013 was appointed as the [[Premier of South Australia|South Australia Premier's]] Professorial Research Fellow in Clean Technology.<ref name = FlindersBio /> Raston is also the founding co-chair of the RACI Green and Sustainable Chemistry (GASC) National Group.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Green and Sustainable Group |url=https://raci.org.au/RACI/Web/About-Us/Divisions/Green%20and%20Sustainable%20Chemistry%20National%20Group.aspx?Code=GASC |access-date=2023-02-27 |website=raci.org.au |language=en}}</ref>

In 2018, Raston was elected Fellow of the [[Australian Academy of Science]] (FAA).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.science.org.au/fellowship/fellows/professor-colin-raston|title=Professor Colin Raston|website=www.science.org.au|access-date=2018-06-16}}</ref>
